query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Low-temperature annealing of as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys reduces chemical and structural inhomogeneities, thereby narrowing the distribution of local exchange interactions that govern the magnetostructural transition. This homogenization should produce a smoother magnetocaloric response with reduced hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys with a disordered microstructure and heterogeneous chemical short-range order leading to a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment, held below the order-disorder transition temperature for a calibrated duration, to promote microstructural homogenization without complete phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Annealing should be performed at a temperature sufficiently low to avoid full diffusion or phase separation yet high enough to relieve internal stresses, and the magnetocaloric properties should be measured under low-applied magnetic fields mimicking cooling cycle conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree and uniformity of chemical short-range order and residual stresses at grain boundaries and interfaces within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment relieves internal stresses and reduces compositional fluctuations, leading to a narrower distribution of magnetostructural transition barriers. This homogenization of exchange interactions smooths the entropy change and reduces hysteretic losses during magnetic cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples are expected to display reduced magnetic hysteresis (evident via lower coercivity and a more gradual change in magnetization) and a broader, less abrupt magnetocaloric response, albeit with a potential modest reduction in the peak entropy change.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloy films that exhibit a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition with limited heat-exchange rates due to low surface-to-volume ratio.
generation.boundary: The predictions are expected to hold for non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys processed under similar deposition conditions; results may differ in bulk, arc-melted, or other structurally distinct forms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in hysteresis and the potential trade-off between peak entropy change and reduced energy dissipation remain uncertain and will require optimization of the annealing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of non-equiatated FeMnNiGeSi alloy samples: one set remains as-deposited while the other undergoes the specified low-temperature annealing. Under identical low-applied magnetic field conditions, measure the magnetization and extract the magnetic entropy change as a function of temperature.
measurements: Magnetization hysteresis curves to assess coercivity and loop area
Temperature dependence of magnetic entropy change (ΔSm)
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to evaluate microstructural homogenization and chemical short-range order
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in magnetic hysteresis and display no measurable microstructural or chemical homogenization compared to the as-deposited samples, then the hypothesis—that microstructural homogenization governs hysteresis and the magnetocaloric response—would be falsified.

Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. However, and despite extensive work on the metallurgical, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties of the nonequiatomic FeMnCoCr system, there is limited work dedicated to investigating the physical properties,. Most of the studies on magnetic and electrical properties of high entropy alloys focus on equiatomic FeCoCrNiX alloy (i.e., derivatives of the FeCoCrNiMn Cantor alloy) where X is Mn, Ti, Cu, or Pd and non-equiatomic FeCoCrNi with slight doping of Al, Cu, and Si. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. More interestingly, the anti-invar property of this alloy which in turn induces strong magnetism in this alloy has been recently reported pointing to a potential for magnetism related applications.
